ZHETALIS NASA GAME - RESOURCE LINKS AND COMPLETE LOCAL SOURCE LIST
Compiled: 15 November 2026 (Asia/Singapore)
Output: C:\NASA\Zhetalis-Nasa\NASA-RESOURCES-USED.txt

Scope: project source, credits, provenance records and downloaded selections in
the main checkout and the animation, co-op, dust and Unity sibling checkouts.
The separate archive lists everything pulled, not only what gameplay loads.
A retained model or reference does not by itself prove an active gameplay use.
No new models were downloaded to produce this inventory. API keys are excluded.
Saved website navigation and the complete unselected OSDR study index are not
counted as resources used. The selected study records and supporting files are.
Download counts/hashes come from existing manifests; file presence was checked
during this export. The large asset archive was not rehashed or render-tested.

CONTENTS
1. Main NASA services and source hubs
2. Game model, terrain and source-provenance highlights
3. All 257 archived GLB model names and download links
4. Scientific datasets, imagery, map tiles and reference downloads
5. All selected OSDR supporting-file downloads
6. Complete NASA asset archive: every file and original URL
7. Other NASA links recorded in project source and data
8. Related non-NASA sources (CSA and NOAA)
9. Unique URL index and evidence paths
10. Inventory notes, link checks and source manifests

==============================================================================
1. MAIN NASA SERVICES AND SOURCE HUBS
==============================================================================

01. NASA Open APIs
https://api.nasa.gov/
API directory originally supplied by the user.

02. NASA DONKI
https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/tools/DONKI/
Historical space-weather events and research references.

03. DONKI API documentation
https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI/api/
Exact event queries are listed in the research downloads.

04. NASA Open Science Data Repository
https://osdr.nasa.gov/bio/repo/
Selected crop, microbial and spacecraft-bioburden studies.

05. OSDR API reference
https://www.nasa.gov/osdr-api/
Study metadata and file catalogues.

06. NASA RadLab API guide
https://visualization.osdr.nasa.gov/radlab/gui/data-api/
Radiation measurements with instrument and location context.

07. RadLab data endpoint
https://visualization.osdr.nasa.gov/radlab/api/
Exact ISS, Mars and lunar-orbit snapshot queries are listed below.

08. Mars Trek
https://trek.nasa.gov/mars/
Map context; archived Viking colour tiles.

09. Mars Trek API documentation
https://trek.nasa.gov/tiles/apidoc/trekAPI.html?body=mars
WMTS layer and map access reference.

10. NASA 3D Resources
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/
Official model landing pages.

11. NASA 3D source repository
https://github.com/nasa/NASA-3D-Resources
Pinned archive of models, printable files, textures and previews.

12. NASA Image and Video Library
https://images.nasa.gov/
Mission, launch, rover, plant and habitat imagery.

13. NASA Image Library API
https://images-api.nasa.gov/
Search metadata and downloadable image asset catalogues.

14. NASA Eyes on the Solar System
https://eyes.nasa.gov/apps/solar-system/#/sc_artemis_2
Orion / Artemis II model source.

15. NASA PGDA LOLA south-pole terrain
https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/products/81
Source of the regional Moon elevation grid.

16. NASA SVS topographic Moon
https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/14959/
LRO topographic Moon model used in flybys.

17. NASA ARES Apollo sample 10017,15
https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/astromaterials3d/sample-details.htm?sample=10017-15
Apollo 11 basalt educational replica.

2. GAME MODEL, TERRAIN AND SOURCE-PROVENANCE HIGHLIGHTS
==============================================================================

Z-2 spacesuit / articulated gameplay derivative
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/z2-spacesuit/
Local evidence/use: game/assets/models/nasa-spacesuits/z2-gameplay.glb; game/src/z2-suit.js; source-assets/blender/z2-gameplay/README.md

NASA astronaut reference / earlier game suit
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/astronaut/
Local evidence/use: game/assets/astronaut.glb; game/assets/nasa-astronaut.glb; earlier suit source retained

JSC Mission Control Room / console source
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/jsc-mission-control-room/
Local evidence/use: game/assets/training/jsc-mission-control-source.json; retained training/briefing console source

Habitat Demonstration Unit / earlier shelter source
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/habitat-demonstration-unit/
Local evidence/use: game/assets/training/shelter-source.json; retained model, not proof that Earth training remains enabled

Spirit landing-site reference
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/mars-spirit-landing-site/
Local evidence/use: game/src/nasamodels.js; earlier Gusev height-source reference

Mars globe / arrival map reference
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/mars/
Local evidence/use: game/src/nasamodels.js; game/assets/mars-map.jpg

Mars MOLA elevation product
https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/missions/mgs/megdr.html
Local evidence/use: game/assets/terrain/gusev-mola-128.json; NASA PDS data hosted by Washington University

Moon regional LOLA elevation data
https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/products/81
Local evidence/use: game/moon/data/regional-terrain.json; 5 m regional grid source

Full topographic Moon and phone derivative
https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/14959/
Local evidence/use: game/assets/nasa/moon-lro.glb; game/assets/nasa/moon-lro-lite.glb

NASA Eyes Orion / Artemis II
https://eyes.nasa.gov/apps/solar-system/#/sc_artemis_2
Local evidence/use: game/assets/nasa/orion/source-manifest.json; orion-eyes.glb

Printable Orion capsule source
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/orion-capsule/
Local evidence/use: game/assets/nasa/orion-capsule.stl; earlier mesh retained

Apollo Lunar Module
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/apollo-lunar-module/
Local evidence/use: game/assets/nasa/apollo-lunar-module.glb; Moon/history exhibit

Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
https://science.nasa.gov/3d-resources/lunar-reconnaissance-orbiter-a/
Local evidence/use: game/assets/nasa/lro-orbiter.glb; lunar survey exhibit

Apollo 11 sample 10017,15
https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/astromaterials3d/sample-details.htm?sample=10017-15
Local evidence/use: game/assets/nasa/apollo-10017-15.glb; game/moon/data/apollo-10017-15.json

Additional game model families recorded in game/assets/README.md and nasamodels.js:
- SLS Block 1, Mobile Launcher and Vehicle Assembly Building.
- Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Ingenuity, Perseverance and MER Opportunity.
- Pistol Grip Tool, Wrench, Crew Lock Bag, Orbital Replacement Unit,
  Infrared Camera and Mark III spacesuit.
Exact original file links and every other archived model are in sections 3 and 6.

Origin distinctions:
- Mars One habitat base: third-party Sketchfab model by admone, not a NASA model.
  https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/mars-one-mission-base-83ced347037f47aba8473147d65df074
- Saturn V history GLB: Stanley Creative / user-supplied, not an official NASA model.
  https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/saturn-v-nasa-7a2c9709ff8144c8b3b18ec84b5e112e
- Cabin characters and their animations: Mixamo; Zhetalis space-pack models:
  original team work. Procedural Starship/HLS geometry is game-authored.

0020. PIA26045.jpg
    URL: http://images-assets.nasa.gov/image/PIA26045/PIA26045~orig.jpg

    Notes: {"title": "SWIM Map Shows Subsurface Water Ice on Mars", "credit": "NASA/JPL-Caltech/Planetary Science Institute", "description": "The blue areas on this map of Mars show regions where NASA missions have detected subsurface water ice. Scientists can use the map – part of the Subsurface Water Ice Mapping project, or SWIM – to decide where the first astronauts to set foot on the Red Planet should land. Triangles on the map are past and present Mars missions; circles are ice-exposing impact craters. Mars has both water ice and carbon dioxide ice (dry ice); water ice would be a critical resource for the first astronauts to step foot on Mars, who can use it for drinking, rocket fuel, and other purposes. The more water ice these astronauts land next to, the less they need to bring with them. Because the Martian atmosphere is so thin – less than 1% the pressure experienced at sea level on Earth – liquid water is unstable on the Red Planet and will vaporize unless it's frozen. But water ice on the planet's surface is only stable at high latitudes that are far too cold for astronauts and robots to survive. So SWIM attempts to locate water ice preserved within the subsurface in the mid-latitudes, where landing would be feasible. Such regions are far enough toward the pole for water ice to be plentiful, but close enough to the equator to avoid the coldest temperatures seen on Mars. SWIM combines data from several NASA missions, including the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), 2001 Mars Odyssey, and the now-inactive Mars Global Surveyor. The project mapped the area from the equator to 60 degrees north latitude. https://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA26045", "date_created": "2023-10-26T00:00:00Z"}

0026. PIA26041.jpg
    URL: http://images-assets.nasa.gov/image/PIA26041/PIA26041~orig.jpg
    Local: pull/images/PIA26041.jpg
    Status: downloaded; local file present
    Notes: {"title": "The Sound of MOXIE at Work on Mars", "credit": "NASA/JPL-Caltech/CNES/IRAP", "description": "MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment) was launched aboard NASA's Perseverance rover to test a technology for extracting oxygen from the Red Planet's carbon dioxide-rich atmosphere. Audio of MOXIE's air compressor at work on Mars was captured by the microphone on Perseverance's SuperCam instrument on May 27, 2021, the 96th day of the rover's mission. Since Perseverance landed on Mars in 2021, MOXIE generated a total of 122 grams of oxygen – about what a small dog breathes in 10 hours. At its most efficient, MOXIE was able to produce 12 grams of oxygen an hour – twice as much as NASA's original goals for the instrument – at 98% purity or better. On its final, 16th run, on Aug. 7, 2023, the instrument made 9.8 grams of oxygen. MOXIE successfully completed all of its technical requirements and was operated at a variety of conditions throughout a full Mars year, allowing the instrument's developers to learn a great deal about the technology. MOXIE produces molecular oxygen through an electrochemical process that separates one oxygen atom from each molecule of carbon dioxide pumped in from Mars' thin atmosphere. As these gases flow through the system, they're analyzed to check the purity and quantity of oxygen produced. While many of Perseverance's experiments are addressing primary science goals, MOXIE was focused on future human exploration. MOXIE served as the first-ever demonstration of technology that humans could use to survive on, and leave, the Red Planet. An oxygen-producing system could help future missions in various ways, but the most important of them would be as a source of rocket propellant, which would be required in industrial quantities to launch rockets with astronauts for their return trip home. Rather than bringing large quantities of oxygen with them to Mars, future astronauts could live off the land, using materials they find on the planet's surface to survive. This concept – called in-situ resource utilization, or ISRU – has evolved into a growing area of research. A key objective for Perseverance's mission on Mars is astrobiology, including the search for signs of ancient microbial life. The rover will characterize the planet's geology and past climate, pave the way for human exploration of the Red Planet, and be the first mission to collect and cache Martian rock and regolith (broken rock and dust). Subsequent NASA missions, in cooperation with ESA (European Space Agency), would send spacecraft to Mars to collect these sealed samples from the surface and return them to Earth for in-depth analysis. The Mars 2020 Perseverance mission is part of NASA's Moon to Mars exploration approach, which includes Artemis missions to the Moon that will help prepare for human exploration of the Red Planet. Audio file available at https://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA26041", "date_created": "2023-09-06T00:00:00Z"}

It also provided demonstrations of new equipment to help prepare for advanced microgravity research and processing aboard the Space Station. Since fluids behave differently in microgravity, plant watering systems that operate well on Earth do not function effectively in space. Plants can reduce the costs of providing food, oxygen, and pure water, as well as lower the costs of removing carbon dioxide in human space habitats.
